name: Alkaline water / alkaline diet
lead: The alkaline diet is a group of loosely related eating patterns built on the idea that foods leave acidic or alkaline residues that shift the body's pH. It favours most fruit and vegetables and limits grains, meat, cheese and eggs. Alkaline water, made with ionizer machines or sold bottled at a raised pH, is promoted on a similar premise.[1][2] It is also called the acid-alkaline, alkaline-ash or acid-ash diet, and in the water form, ionized water.[1][2]

People adopt these approaches hoping for a clearer, glowing complexion, slower visible aging, a leaner body and more energy. The route is indirect: a plate built around fruit and vegetables displaces processed foods, which followers expect to bring lower calorie intake and healthier-looking skin and physique.[1] The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics review cited by Wikipedia found elements such as eating green leafy vegetables likely healthy.[1] In strength-training circles the vocabulary appears in cleanses, lemon-water routines and lean-physique advice.[8][11][12]

The pH theory itself is contested. Reviews report that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH in healthy people, which is tightly regulated within a narrow range around 7.35 to 7.45, and that urine pH does not reflect overall body acidity.[1][13] Research on alkaline water has examined athletic and metabolic outcomes rather than appearance.[3][4][5][7] The best-known promoter, Robert O. Young, has been the subject of criminal and civil proceedings.[9]

paras: Versions of the diet differ, but most rank foods by supposed alkaline or acid-forming effect and encourage the alkaline group. Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, cheese and grains are classed as acid-producing and most fruits and vegetables as alkaline-producing; citrus counts as alkaline despite being acidic, because the classification rests on the residue left when food is burned rather than on the taste.[1] Advocates sometimes recommend testing urine or saliva pH to track progress, a practice Wikipedia says does not reflect overall body pH.[1]

Food lists differ between sources. A common version treats most vegetables, fruit, herbs and some nuts as alkalizing and meat, dairy, refined grains and sugar as acidifying. Wikipedia explains the underlying idea as the acid-ash hypothesis: anions such as chloride, phosphate and sulfate were presumed acid-forming and cations such as potassium, calcium and magnesium base-forming, with cranberries, prunes and plums as exceptions because hippuric acid makes urine more acidic.[1]

For appearance, followers cite a clearer, brighter complexion, slower visible ageing, a leaner body and more energy as the payoffs. The reasoning chain is that a plant-heavy plate raises the proportion of fruit and vegetables and drops processed foods, which may lead to lower calorie intake and a healthier-looking skin and physique.[1]

Alternative-medicine practitioners promote the diet through websites, books, magazines and direct mail, and many promoters also sell supplements and courses.[1] Robert O. Young's The pH Miracle series offers it as a weight-loss method, according to Wikipedia; Lalita Kaul's review for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics found parts of it likely healthy while concluding that its reliance on fasting and supplements makes it not a healthy way to lose weight.[1] Wikipedia describes the diet as demanding in effort because so many foods are excluded.[1]

Marketers of ionized water say it can slow aging, offset acidic foods or hydrate better after exercise.[2] A 2022 review of electrolyzed-reduced water argued that observed effects of such water are explained by dissolved molecular hydrogen rather than by alkalinity or other proposed properties.[6]

A water ionizer is a home appliance that uses electrolysis across an ion-exchange membrane to split incoming water into an alkaline stream and an acidic stream. Wikipedia describes machines that also produce calcium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid, and says the devices became popular in Japan and other East Asian countries before reaching the US and Europe.[2] Marketers claim the water slows ageing, prevents disease, boosts energy, offsets acidic foods and hydrates better after exercise, and some claim electrolysis forms smaller water 'micro clusters' that the body absorbs more readily; Wikipedia states that there is no empirical evidence for these claims.[2]

Wikipedia also reports that drinking alkaline water is not expected to change body pH because of acid-base homeostasis, and that several cancer societies reject the idea that alkaline intake prevents cancer.[2] Bottled alkaline water is a related product sold at raised pH, often with added minerals.[2]

Wikipedia describes electrolysis in these home machines as slow and power-hungry, so that a fast-flowing tap stream would yield little hydroxide, and says that if the alkaline and acidic streams are only partly separated they can recombine into near-neutral water.[2] A 2022 review of electrolyzed-reduced water, written by researchers who study molecular hydrogen, argued that benefits seen in studies should be credited to dissolved hydrogen gas, and described other proposed properties such as 'micro clusters' and 'free electrons' as unsupported.[6] Supporters of ionized water point to its use in Japan and East Asia, where the machines were first popular.[2]

In the 1800s Claude Bernard observed that rabbits switched from plants to meat produced more acidic urine, and later researchers burned foods in a bomb calorimeter and treated the leftover ash as a guide to whether a food was acid- or base-forming, which gave rise to the dietary ash hypothesis.[1] In the early twentieth century attention shifted to anions and cations, and cranberries, prunes and plums were found to acidify urine because of hippuric acid.[1] The hypothesis was mainly developed in research on osteoporosis.[1]

Alkaline diets were historically used to manage urine pH for kidney stones and urinary infections; Wikipedia says medications later replaced them because the effect of diet on urine pH is hard to predict.[1] A 2011 clinical trial examined how manipulating food materials changed urine pH and uric acid excretion.[10]

A separate earlier current was food combining. New York physician William Howard Hay developed his diet in the 1920s after changes in eating and giving up coffee and smoking improved his own hypertension and kidney disease. He sorted foods into 'alkaline', 'acid' and 'neutral' groups, kept protein and starch in separate meals, and the diet was fashionable in the 1930s, with followers reportedly including Henry Ford and Man Ray.[14] Wikipedia says Hay's use of the words does not match their chemical meaning, that the Journal of the American Medical Association called him a food faddist, and that only one peer-reviewed randomised trial of the diet has been found, reporting no weight-loss benefit.[14] Variants such as the Beverly Hills Diet and the Kensington diet descended from it.[14]

Systematic reviews in the 2010s examined the bone claim directly. Wikipedia cites Fenton and colleagues' 2011 meta-analysis, which applied Hill's criteria for causality, and Hanley and Whiting's 2013 review; both are described as failing to support the idea that acid-forming diets cause bone loss.[1] Remer (2000), cited there, found that urine pH cannot yet be predicted precisely from diet.[1]

Robert O. Young, an American naturopath born in 1952, is the best-known author of the pH Miracle series, which holds that the body is 'alkaline by design and acidic by function' and that illness stems from acidity; he teaches that disease is essentially one condition, acidosis, and also promotes live blood analysis.[9] Wikipedia reports that his naturopathy and nutrition doctorates came from an unaccredited correspondence school and that he is not a medical doctor.[9] It records a plea to a reduced charge in Utah in the 1990s, a 2016 conviction on two counts of practising medicine without a licence, a 2017 plea deal and a sentence of 44 months, a 2018 San Diego civil jury award of $105 million to a cancer patient that the judge later reduced to about $25 million, and a 2025 conviction for elder abuse, theft and unlicensed practice.[9] It also describes the case of Kim Tinkham, who promoted his protocols on a US television show in 2008 and died in 2010.[9] His history is part of the context in which dietitians and cancer charities discuss the diet.[1][9]

Bodybuilding and strength forums discuss alkalinity mainly through nutrition and cleanse habits. A 2009 post in a T Nation thread on the Anabolic Diet suggested adding lemon or lime juice to water through the day to keep the body 'more alkaline', and a 2006 poster described a weekly lemon-juice and cayenne-water fast because lemon juice is 'very alkaline'.[11][8] A 2016 thread quoted strength coach Charles Poliquin's advice to begin the day with a meat-and-nut breakfast and limit dairy, a high-protein pattern that alkaline-diet lists class as acid-forming.[12][1]

In 2018 the British Dietetic Association included the alkaline diet in its list of celebrity diets to avoid, alongside raw vegan and ketogenic regimes, according to Wikipedia.[1] The diet is often discussed together with the Hay diet's alkaline and acid food groups and with other cleanses.[14]

Lifter forums mix the alkaline idea with other nutrition ideas. A T Nation poster in a 2007 thread mentioned being on an 'alkaline diet' and being asked whether grains were still eaten, linking it to back pain; another, in a 2008 training log, complained that a high-fat, low-carb diet 'lacks alkalinity' and suggested green tea and water.[15][16]

A 2013 review by Hanley and Whiting found that, in healthy people, changes in diet have never been shown to disturb blood pH or bicarbonate, and that the predicted metabolic acidosis has remained hypothetical; blood pH is held between 7.35 and 7.45.[1] Wikipedia reports that urine pH does not reflect overall body acidity.[1] A systematic review in BMJ Open found no link between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer, and the American Institute for Cancer Research and the Canadian Cancer Society are quoted as rejecting the cancer claim.[1][2]

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics said parts of the diet such as eating leafy greens and exercising are likely healthy, while the British Dietetic Association placed it on a 2018 list of celebrity diets it criticised.[1] Excluding food groups can risk nutrient deficiencies, including fatty acids and phytonutrients, and cancer patients are cautioned about extreme diets.[1]

Wikipedia's article on acid-base homeostasis describes three lines of defence that hold blood pH in its narrow range: chemical buffers (bicarbonate being the main one in extracellular fluid), breathing, which changes carbon dioxide levels, and the kidneys, which excrete acid and conserve bicarbonate.[13] Dietitians' position, as reported by Wikipedia, is that diet can change urine pH but not produce a lasting change in blood pH.[1]

Supporters answer in several ways. Many frame the diet as a way to eat more plants rather than as a literal pH intervention, and the 2017 exercise review itself noted that a more alkaline dietary pattern may suit overall health because diet-induced acidosis has been associated with cardiovascular and bone disease.[3] Ionizer sellers point to the machines' popularity in Japan and East Asia, while reviewers of electrolyzed water attribute observed effects to dissolved molecular hydrogen.[2][6]

No studies found testing alkaline water or the alkaline diet for skin or appearance outcomes. A 2017 review of ten studies on dietary acid load and exercise found that lower acid loads raised plasma pH but did not consistently improve performance, while suggesting a more alkaline dietary pattern may suit overall health.[3] A 2024 trial in 22 trained athletes combined an alkalizing diet with bicarbonate-rich water or placebo over a simulated three-day 400 m race.[4] A 2024 randomised trial in boxing athletes examined alkaline water with L-glutamine and reported higher salivary alpha-amylase and testosterone concentrations.[5] A 2011 clinical trial examined food manipulation of urine pH and uric acid excretion.[10] A 2025 pilot trial examined electrolysed alkaline water in hyperuricemia.[7]

A 2024 randomised study of alkaline water with conventional drugs in chronic gouty arthritis, published in the journal Medicine, was later retracted, with a retraction notice published the same year.[17][18]

lore.intro: Alkaline eating and water appear in training and wellness forums as part of detox, cleanse and leanness routines, usually as short tips rather than structured protocols.[8][11][12][15]

claims.claim: Alkaline foods and water change body pH and improve health and looks
claims.believers: Proponents say alkaline foods counter acidity, and a T Nation poster described a weekly lemon juice and cayenne water fast partly because lemon juice is alkaline.[8]
claims.experts: Reviews report that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH in healthy people, and urine pH does not reflect overall body acidity.[1]

claims.claim: Alkaline water hydrates better or aids exercise recovery
claims.believers: Ionizer marketers say it hydrates better after exercise.[2]
claims.experts: Small athlete trials have examined alkaline water, with mixed performance findings, and a 2017 review did not find consistent performance benefits from lower dietary acid loads.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: The alkaline diet slows aging or prevents cancer
claims.believers: Marketers of ionized water say it can slow aging.[2]
claims.experts: A BMJ Open systematic review found no link between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer.[2]

claims.claim: Lemon water and citrus make the body alkaline
claims.believers: Posters in training forums say lemon or lime in water keeps the body 'more alkaline' and helps cleanses.[11][8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes citrus is classed alkaline in the diet's scheme because of the ash left on burning, and that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH.[1]

claims.claim: Cutting acid-forming foods (meat, dairy, grains) gives clearer skin and a leaner body
claims.believers: Followers report brighter skin and weight loss when they move to a plant-heavy pattern, and strength-sport posters reach for 'alkaline' routines when cutting.[1][16]
claims.experts: No published study was found testing alkaline eating for skin or appearance outcomes; the Academy review said the plant-heavy elements are likely healthy while its fasting and supplements are not a healthy way to lose weight.[1]

claims.claim: Acidity causes cancer and an alkaline body prevents it
claims.believers: Young's pH Miracle holds that acidity underlies illness, and ionizer marketers link alkaline intake to cancer prevention.[2][9]
claims.experts: Cancer societies and a BMJ Open systematic review report no link; Wikipedia notes tumour growth itself produces acidity, not the reverse.[1][2]

claims.claim: Testing urine or saliva pH shows how acidic your body is
claims.believers: Advocates recommend pH strips to track progress on the diet.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says urine pH does not reflect overall body acidity, and the kidneys vary it as part of normal regulation.[1][13]

claims.claim: Electrolysis makes water 'micro-clustered' so it hydrates more effectively
claims.believers: Ionizer marketers claim smaller water clusters are absorbed more readily.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states there is no empirical evidence for this, and a 2022 review rejects the cluster explanation while crediting dissolved hydrogen for observed effects.[2][6]

card.summary: Diet and water pH claims that dietitians and cancer charities say do not change blood pH; no appearance studies exist.
card.note: Restrictive versions can cause nutrient gaps; cost of ionizers and supplements.

quick.overview:
The alkaline diet and alkaline water rest on the idea that what you eat or drink shifts body pH and thereby health. The diet favours plants and excludes most animal foods and grains.

Reviews report no evidence that diet changes blood pH in healthy people, and no appearance studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say foods leave acidic or alkaline residues that affect the body; physiologists note blood pH is tightly regulated, and urine pH does not reflect body acidity.
quick.risks: Excluding food groups can cause nutrient deficiencies, and cancer organisations caution against relying on it; promoters often sell supplements and equipment.

chain: Eat mostly fruit and vegetables and drink alkaline or ionized water
Shift toward a plant-heavy, lower-processed pattern
Claimed: clearer skin, leaner body, more energy
angle.text: Followers use alkaline foods and water hoping for a brighter complexion, less visible aging and easier weight control. The plant-forward food list is the part of the diet that dietitians describe as likely healthy; the pH-shifting mechanism is the part that reviews do not support.
